details:
The AlgoBeat team developed two web prototypes that combine scientific visualization and sonification to offer a sensory experience focused on inclusion. The project addresses The Earth Information Jukebox challenge by exploring how visually presented information can also be perceived through sound.

The first prototype translates features of scientific images into sound parameters through explainable mappings. An object’s distance from the center of the image controls pitch, its brightness controls volume, and its horizontal position determines whether the sound is heard on the left or right. Different scanning modes change the sequence of notes. The exploration of galaxy fields also includes a 3D mode with spatial audio, allowing users to navigate a sonic representation of the image.

The second prototype, Earth Time Machine, provides an interactive globe with NASA GIBS imagery. Users select layers and dates, explore a timeline, and use continuous playback to observe changes in Earth visualizations. In its sonification, latitude controls pitch, the value used by the application controls volume, and whether an anomaly is classified as warm or cold guides the musical scale. Real-time sound generation can use historical imagery, with date availability varying by layer.

The intended benefit is to broaden participation in scientific experiences. The project could support lessons, workshops, museums, planetariums, and science communication activities, giving students and other audiences additional ways to explore patterns. Blind people and people with low vision are part of this audience, and their involvement in development will be important for evaluating comprehension and guiding improvements.

The creative approach combines spatial exploration, the passage of time, and musical choices linked to the source material. We considered the clarity of the mappings, the scientific interpretation of the imagery, and the balance between information and artistic experience. Our goal is to help users understand which features cause changes in the sound.

Both prototypes use web interfaces. Earth Time Machine packages the application in a single file, uses NASA GIBS services, and adopts the AGPL license. Programming languages, libraries, and development tools: [insert the technologies actually used].

We have not yet conducted user testing, and the image sonification interface needs improvements to work with screen readers. The next steps include documenting the technical mappings, demonstrating the processing of specific EIC frames, publishing the prototypes, and evaluating them with diverse participants. Future possibilities include installations with spatial audio and a tactile globe that represents ocean temperatures through sensations of warmth and cold.
